clips.stepText: Two people can lift the same load and finish at different times. Power tells you who transferred the energy faster. If you do six joules of work in two seconds, that is three watts. Watch for minutes hiding in the question.

clips.stepText: You can gain force by moving your hand farther than the load moves. If a two newton pull lifts six newtons, the force gain is three. Suppose your hand travels four times farther. Then three quarters of the input work reaches the load.

clips.stepText: A longer handle lets your hand move farther for the same turn. Put your hand two metres from the pivot and the load one metre away. Your hand moves twice as far for a small turn. An ideal lever then needs half the load force.

clips.stepText: The machine helps because your end moves farther than the load. If two rope sections shorten together, pulling in four metres lifts the block two metres. For a ramp, compare the whole path with the rise. You use that same distance trade each time.

clips.stepText: The three hundred joules describe the whole job. We need the amount per second, so spread that energy over the three seconds. You get one hundred watts of useful output for the lift.

clips.stepText: You know how far each side moves compared with the other. For the same turn, the effort side travels twice as far. Write that ratio first. We will need the efficiency to find how much of the ideal force gain survives.

clips.stepText: The load is the bigger force here, so divide it by the gain. You get one hundred newtons. Check the direction of the division by multiplying that effort by one point eight to recover the load.

clips.stepText: A weight can press gently over a wide patch or hard on one spot. Put four newtons over two square metres and you get two pascals. To compare how tightly packed materials are, use mass and volume instead. You can compare that density with water.

clips.stepText: A deeper point supports more liquid above it. That is why we measure depth from the surface. Take one metre of water and gravity at ten metres per second squared. The water adds ten thousand pascals. Add air pressure only when asked for the full pressure.

clips.stepText: A narrow piston lets you create pressure with a small push. The enclosed liquid passes that change along. If the other piston has twice the area, a two newton push can produce four newtons there. The wider piston moves only half as far.

clips.stepText: A submerged object makes room for liquid that used to be there. Weigh that missing liquid to find the upward push. If it would weigh two newtons and the object weighs five, a supporting scale shows three newtons. Keep the two weights separate.

clips.stepText: A floating object settles where the water pushes up just enough. A block with half the water's density needs only half its volume underwater. The other half can stay in air. Use the average density of the whole floating object.

clips.stepText: Imagine a narrow column of water reaching down to the point. A deeper column has more weight for the same base area. Multiply the density, gravity and depth to turn that weight per area into pressure.

clips.stepText: The change in the reading is the clue to the upward push. The scale gives two mass equivalents, so find the gap first. In water it reads eight kilograms less than in air. The force itself must be in newtons.

clips.stepText: The weight supported by the scale fell because the water helped hold the object up. Multiply that gap by the given gravity. The water supplies eighty newtons of support while the scale supplies the rest.

clips.stepText: The same temperature can get different numbers on different scales. Think of melting ice at zero Celsius. On the Kelvin scale it reads two hundred and seventy three point one five. A one degree Celsius rise is still a one kelvin rise.

clips.stepText: An echo stopwatch runs all the way out and back. If a pulse covers six hundred metres in that time, the wall is three hundred metres away. One clear return is an echo. Many overlapping returns make the sound linger.

clips.stepText: A string or pipe responds strongly when a repeating push fits one of its patterns. The end conditions tell you which patterns fit. A pipe one metre long with one closed end fits a four metre fundamental wave. The closed end cannot move freely.

clips.stepText: You can raise a string's note by stretching it tighter. A tighter string carries the wave faster. Raise the tension from four newtons to sixteen. Keep the length and string the same. The frequency only doubles. Watch for the square root in that change.

clips.stepText: A passing okada can sound higher before it reaches you. Imagine two successive crests leaving a moving source. The second starts closer to you while it approaches, so the gaps ahead shrink. If you receive three crests a second instead of two, the note sounds higher.

clips.stepText: The question wants a one way distance, so notice what the stopwatch actually times. It starts at the shout and stops when the echo returns. So the sound has travelled to the wall and back again. Keep that in mind, because we will need to halve at the end.

clips.stepText: You know how far the sound travels each second. Multiply by the time it spends on both legs. That gives six hundred and eighty metres of travel. See that we have counted the route towards the wall and back.

clips.stepText: The wall stays in one place, so the two legs are equal in this setup. Split the total into two equal parts. The wall is three hundred and forty metres away from the person who shouted.

clips.stepText: Start with the ends because they tell you what shape the air can make. The closed end holds the air still there. At the opening, the air can swing back and forth freely. That gives you a quarter of a wavelength in the pipe.

clips.stepText: You only have the shortest piece of the wave that fits between these two ends. Four such lengths make a complete wave. Use metres for the pipe length and you get one point eight metres for the wavelength.

clips.stepText: The speed tells how many metres the pattern moves each second. Each wave takes up one point eight metres, so divide to count how many waves pass per second. You get two hundred hertz.

clips.stepText: A compression and a neighbouring rarefaction show opposite parts of the pattern. Look for the next compression to complete the wave. Doubling the given gap gives zero point three four metres. Then divide the speed by that full wavelength.

clips.stepText: Look into the bowl of a shiny spoon. Your face can turn upside down as it moves away. The curved surface sends light back in different directions.

clips.stepText: You need one steady line to compare incoming and outgoing light. Draw it at a right angle where the ray hits. A ray thirty degrees from that line leaves thirty degrees on the other side. The mirror surface gives a different angle.

clips.stepText: A screen can catch light only where the rays themselves meet. If a concave mirror has a radius of two metres, parallel rays meet one metre away. Bring your face closer than that point. Then the rays spread, and you see an upright virtual image.

clips.stepText: You need signs because the same formula handles real and virtual images. Start a real object two metres from a converging device of focal length one metre. The image forms two metres away. The minus in the magnification tells you it is upside down.

clips.stepText: A ray can bend because it changes speed at a boundary. If light travels at half its vacuum speed in a material, the index is two. When a slanting ray enters it from air, the ray bends closer to the normal.

clips.stepText: At some boundaries, all the light can bounce back. Check that it is heading towards a lower index first. At the limiting angle, it skims the boundary. From an index of two into air, that angle is thirty degrees. A larger angle gives total internal reflection.

clips.stepText: A submerged object can look closer because your eye traces bent rays back in straight lines. Look almost straight down through a liquid of index two from air. Something two metres below the surface then looks about one metre below it.

clips.stepText: We need the image position and its size compared with the object. First, mark the lens as converging, so its focal length is positive. The object is real, so its distance is positive too. Write both in metres before you put them into the lens formula.

clips.stepText: The positive distance puts the real image on the far side of the lens. The size ratio has magnitude one, so the image matches the object's size. Its minus sign tells you the top becomes the bottom.

clips.stepText: The word real tells you where the rays meet, so choose a positive image distance. The image size is four times the object size. That means the image distance is four times the object distance in this sign convention.

clips.stepText: You can use one unknown because both distances are tied together. A whole reciprocal and a quarter reciprocal make five quarters. Use that to turn the equation into a direct statement about the object distance.

clips.stepText: You get fifteen centimetres, just beyond the focal point. That fits a real, enlarged image on the far side. Its distance is sixty centimetres from the lens. The negative magnification confirms the image is upside down.

clips.stepText: An enlarged face still needs to look upright when you shave. Between the focus and the centre of curvature, the rays meet and turn the image upside down. Move your face inside the focus to see the enlarged upright version.

clips.stepText: The image looks as though it is behind the glass, but that does not stretch it. The plane mirror places it as far back as you stand in front. Its height stays the same, so the size ratio is one.

clips.stepText: You are at a junction with two open roads. People can split between them and meet again later. An electrical circuit can offer charge more than one route.
clips.mathToSpeechText: You are at a junction with two open roads. People can split between them and meet again later. An electrical circuit can offer charge more than one route.

clips.stepText: You need two measurements to describe what a circuit does. Two coulombs passing in one second make two amps. If those charges transfer six joules, each coulomb transfers three joules. That makes three volts. One number describes flow, the other energy per charge.

clips.stepText: To predict the flow, see how much the path resists it. Four volts across two ohms drive two amps. Keep the temperature fixed. If twice the voltage gives twice the current, you have what we call an ohmic conductor.

clips.stepText: A series path gives charge no choice about where to go. Each resistor gets the same current, so each adds its own voltage drop. Put two ohms and three ohms in that one path. Together they behave like five ohms.
clips.mathToSpeechText: A series path gives charge no choice about where to go. Each resistor gets the same current, so each adds its own voltage drop. Put two ohms and three ohms in that one path. Together they behave like five ohms.

clips.stepText: Another branch gives charge another way across. Each branch sees the same voltage, but each carries its own current. Two equal branches of two ohms together behave like one ohm. Notice how adding a path reduces the resistance.
clips.mathToSpeechText: Another branch gives charge another way across. Each branch sees the same voltage, but each carries its own current. Two equal branches of two ohms together behave like one ohm. Notice how adding a path reduces the resistance.

clips.stepText: A cell can lose some of its push inside itself once charge flows. Suppose its open circuit reading is six volts. One amp through two ohms inside the cell costs two volts. You then measure four volts across the outside terminals.

clips.stepText: A longer wire gives charge a longer path through the material. Widen the wire and you give it more room. If a wire is two ohms, twice the length with the same cross section gives four ohms. Hold the material and temperature fixed.

clips.stepText: We need the voltage that reaches the outside resistor. But some of the cell's push is used up inside the cell whenever current flows. So write down both resistances first. One ohm is inside the cell, and two ohms is outside it.

clips.stepText: The current must pass through the cell's internal resistance and the external resistor in the same loop. Add them before dividing. Six volts across that three ohm path drives two amps through both parts.
clips.mathToSpeechText: The current must pass through the cell's internal resistance and the external resistor in the same loop. Add them before dividing. Six volts across that three ohm path drives two amps through both parts.

clips.stepText: The terminals are on either side of the outside resistor, so work out its share of the voltage. That gives four volts. The other two volts are lost inside the cell, which checks the full six.
clips.mathToSpeechText: The terminals are on either side of the outside resistor, so work out its share of the voltage. That gives four volts. The other two volts are lost inside the cell, which checks the full six.

clips.stepText: First check whether the target is above or below the starting resistance. We want less than two hundred ohms, so we need to give charge another path. A positive resistor placed along the same route would increase the total.

clips.stepText: The parallel rule adds the contributions from each branch. Subtract the original branch's contribution from the combined one. You now have one over the new resistance. Make sure you turn that result back over.
clips.mathToSpeechText: The parallel rule adds the contributions from each branch. Subtract the original branch's contribution from the combined one. You now have one over the new resistance. Make sure you turn that result back over.

clips.stepText: To check, put three hundred ohms alongside the original two hundred. The combined value comes out at one hundred and twenty ohms. It is smaller than either branch, which is what we expect with an extra path.

clips.stepText: Look at which wire the question points to before doing any arithmetic. Each branch sees the battery's twelve volts. To find the current in the twelve ohm branch, use just that branch's resistance. The other branches carry their own currents.

clips.stepText: Two appliances can use the same voltage and draw different currents. To compare how fast they take in energy, you need both numbers. Two amps at three volts takes in six watts. That means six joules enter the device each second.

clips.stepText: You can work out heating without knowing both the current and voltage. For two amps in a three ohm resistor, square the two first. Four times three gives twelve watts. At the same resistance, doubling the current makes four times the heat per second.

clips.spokenLine: The meter keeps counting as long as the appliance runs. Five watts for two seconds transfers ten joules. For a bill, you would use kilowatts and hours instead. Notice that a kilowatt hour measures energy, even though its name contains a power unit.

clips.stepText: A meter adds what each appliance uses during its running time. Take two heaters of one kilowatt each for one hour. Together they use two units. At three naira per unit, that energy costs six naira. Use separate times if the appliances ran for different lengths.

clips.stepText: You need the whole amount of energy, so start with how fast it transfers and how long it runs. Power tells you the joules used each second. Eighty watts means eighty joules every second. So we just need to count the seconds.

clips.stepText: The lamp transfers eighty joules each second at its rated power. Count five equal shares of that energy. Look at the units as you multiply. The seconds in the time and the per second in power cancel each other.

clips.stepText: The question asks how much energy moved, so finish in joules. Five shares of eighty make four hundred. If the same lamp ran for ten seconds, the energy would double while its power rating would stay the same.

clips.stepText: The lamps all run for the same time, so you can add their powers before working out the energy. The small lamps together draw two hundred and fifty watts. The large ones draw four hundred. Keep both groups in that total.

clips.stepText: The price is for a kilowatt hour, so use kilowatts with the ten hours. The lamps use a little over half a unit each hour. After ten hours that is six and a half units altogether.

clips.stepText: Now you have something the tariff can price. Pay two kobo for each of those six and a half units. That is thirteen kobo. There are a hundred kobo in a naira, so the answer is thirteen hundredths of a naira.

clips.stepText: Watts count joules each second, so one hour must become seconds before you multiply. There are three thousand six hundred seconds. Keep the sixty watts and the same running time. The larger number comes from switching time units.

clips.stepText: You want the faulty appliance cut off from the supply voltage. A break in neutral stops current round the loop, but parts can stay connected to live. In the exam diagram, look for protection on the live side.

clips.stepText: When a question looks like a bill, ask which quantity the number describes. Watts tell you the rate. The time turns it into energy. Then the price per unit tells you the charge.

clips.stepText: Imagine a pile of beans. Set half aside each round and keep playing with the rest. The same fraction goes each round, even when the pile gets smaller.

clips.stepText: You need to know what left before working out what remains. In an alpha particle, count two protons and two neutrons. That gives four particles from the nucleus. A beta minus particle is an electron. Gamma carries energy away without taking protons or neutrons.

clips.stepText: Checking both rows helps you avoid losing track of the nucleus. Take one alpha away and the top number drops by four. The bottom drops by two. In the example, add those small counts back to check that both rows balance.

clips.stepText: The next interval acts only on the part still there. Start with eight undecayed nuclei in a simple model. One half life leaves four on average. A second leaves two. You halve the new amount each time, so equal times remove unequal amounts.

clips.stepText: To compare samples, you may need the rate of decay now. It falls as the number of undecayed nuclei falls. A source at eight becquerels drops to four after one half life. If you measure it with a counter, remove the background reading first.

clips.stepText: You need radiation to reach the detector in a tracer study. That same ability to travel is why protection matters. If an exposure lasts two seconds instead of four at the same dose rate, it gives half the dose. Distance and suitable shielding help too.

clips.stepText: The question asks for the activity that remains, so we can count how many times it halves. Both times are given in hours, so they compare directly. Every two hours, the activity is cut in half. Now count how many two hour blocks fit into six hours.

clips.stepText: You want to know how many equal intervals fit into the wait. Divide the whole time by one half life. The seconds cancel, leaving three. That number tells you how many times to cut the remaining rate in half.

clips.stepText: Each arrow starts from the rate left after the previous step. Half of eighty is forty, then half of forty is twenty. The third cut leaves ten becquerels. We have used each of the three intervals once.

clips.stepText: The question wants two different numbers in a particular order. Start by separating the total particles in the nucleus from just the protons. Treat the unqualified beta particles as beta minus in this past question. Now follow the two counts separately.

clips.stepText: An alpha takes protons and neutrons out together. Each carries four particles altogether, including two protons. Taking out two alphas removes eight from the total, and four from the proton count. Keep the results in those separate columns.

clips.stepText: A beta minus emission changes a neutron into a proton. Three such changes raise the proton count to ninety one. The total stays at two hundred and twenty seven. Gamma gives off energy, so neither number moves again.

clips.stepText: The trap is stopping after one half life. Twenty seconds only takes one thousand down to five hundred. Keep halving until you reach one hundred and twenty five. That takes three halvings. Three times twenty seconds gives sixty seconds.

clips.stepText: Before dividing the total time, count how many halvings give one sixty fourth. Six does it because two to the sixth is sixty four. A ten year answer would give twelve halvings in this question, leaving far less.
